newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Lange credits anti-nuke law to U.S., France.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Lange credits anti-nuke law to U.S., France.

text.p: New Zealand's controversial 10-year-old anti-nuclear policy might never have become law if the United States and France had not reacted to it with such hostility, former Prime Minister David Lange told Reuters.
"The two countries who did most to seal in the anti-nuclear policy were the United States and France with their reprisals," Lange said. "They set it in place."

He said the aggressive response of the two nuclear powers to New Zealand's anti-nuclear stance -- which turned 10 years old on Sunday -- created a groundswell of national support for it to be enshrined in legislation.
"People were saying...if you give in now to those Americans we'll never dream of voting for you again," he said.
Lange's Labour Party was returned for a second term in government two months after the nuclear-free law was passed.

Premier from 1984 to 1989, Lange championed the anti-nuclear debate by declaring New Zealand a nuclear-free zone and banning all nuclear-armed and nuclear-powered ships from its shores as soon as he took office.
The policy was eventually enshrined in the New Zealand Nuclear Free Zone, Disarmament and Arms Control Act of 1987.
The policy triggered a deep, decade-long rift with the United States, which retaliated by suspending New Zealand from the tripartite ANZUS defence alliance with the U.S. and Australia in 1986.
France had meanwhile sent secret agents to New Zealand in 1985 to blow up Greenpeace flagship the Rainbow Warrior in Auckland Harbour. One crew member was killed in the blast.
Greenpeace and New Zealand were opposed to French nuclear testing at Mururoa Atoll in the South Pacific.

Lange said the actions of both countries exposed the "hypocrisy" of the Western Alliance towards nuclear disarmament and he slammed the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, saying it wasn't worth the paper it was written on.
"The super powers have never done anything on the nuclear issue that inconvenienced them in the slightest way," he said.
"They agreed not to detonate in outer space and underwater because they didn't have to. They've never fixed a date for disarmament, but have always pledged to do it."
However, he said New Zealand's stand against the nuclear powers had earned it the respect of other nations and helped to stiffen global opposition to weapons of mass destruction.

"It was a matter which enhanced New Zealand's standing, not in the nuclear power countries, but in the rest of the world. Certainly in India, in the Asian subcontinent and in Africa there was enormous support for it," he said.
"And what has happened since then of course is that there has been an enormous enthusiasm for people to say that they are nuclear free and anti-nuclear."
Lange said he was proud of New Zealand's nuclear-free law despite the costs.

"It's a development in New Zealand's history which was responsible internally for a surge in nationhood. It had costs in terms of repositioning our defence arrangements, of antagonising friends and allies.
"But we had the right as a sovereign people to determine as a matter of government policy what came onto our shores, and we exercised that right."
